      The interfaces `IB` and `IC` both extend `IA`, and each of them explicitly implements `IA.M` with a
      default body. The class `D` implements both interfaces but does not declare `M` itself. What happens
      when the program is built and run (C# 14, .NET 10)?
    hint: Does either of `IB` and `IC` derive from the other? That decides which implementation of `IA.M` the compiler can map for `D`.
    options:
      a: "The program prints `IB`."
      b: "The program prints `IC`."
      c: "The program builds, and the call `item.M()` throws `System.Runtime.AmbiguousImplementationException`."
      d: "Compile error CS8705."
    optionExplanations:
      a: "The order of interfaces in the base type list does not affect the choice of a default implementation. The first listed interface gets no priority."
      b: "The last listed interface gets no priority either: the selection rule relies on the interface hierarchy, not on the order in the base type list."
      c: "Here all the types are in one compilation, so the compiler sees the conflict and the program does not build. A run-time exception is possible only when the compiler did not see the conflict, for example when the interfaces live in another assembly that was updated without recompiling `D`."
    answer: "Compile error CS8705: the interface member `IA.M` does not have a most specific implementation."
    explanation: |
      To map the interface member `IA.M` for the class `D`, the compiler looks for an implementation in the
      class itself, and if there is none, for the most specific default implementation among the class's
      interfaces. An implementation is the most specific one when its interface derives from the interfaces
      of all the other candidates.

      `IB` and `IC` both extend `IA`, but they are not related to each other, so neither implementation is
      more specific than the other. This is the classic diamond: the compiler cannot pick an implementation
      and reports error CS8705 for the class `D`. The order of interfaces in `class D : IB, IC` does not matter.

      There are two ways to fix it:

      - declare `M` in `D` itself (implicitly, `public void M()`, or explicitly, `void IA.M()`): a class
        implementation always wins over default implementations;
      - add an interface that extends both `IB` and `IC` and implements `IA.M` itself, so its implementation
        becomes the most specific one.

      Inside its own implementation `D` cannot simply call `((IB)this).M()`: for a `D` object that call comes
      back to the implementation in `D` and causes infinite recursion. Shared logic is usually moved into a
      helper method.

      If the interfaces live in a separate assembly and the second implementation appears in a new version of
      it without recompiling `D`, the compiler does not see the conflict, and the runtime detects the ambiguity
      instead: it throws `AmbiguousImplementationException`. The behaviour is described for C# 14 and .NET 10
      and has not changed since default interface methods were added in C# 8.
    linkTitles:
      - "C# 8 proposal: default interface methods"
      - "interface keyword (C# reference)"

    title: Which changes in an overriding method break the Liskov substitution principle?

      The base class `OrderSource` has a virtual method
      `IReadOnlyList<Order> Find(string customerId, int limit)` with this documented contract:

      - caller obligations (preconditions): `customerId` is not `null`, `limit` is from 1 to 100;
      - method guarantees (postconditions): the result is not `null` and contains at most `limit` orders,
        the order of the orders is not guaranteed;
      - exceptions: only `OrderSourceUnavailableException`, when the storage is unavailable.

      Code is written against this contract and receives instances of different derived classes. Which of
      these overrides of `Find` break substituting the derived class for `OrderSource`? Select all that apply.
    hint: For each option ask whether calling code that follows the base class contract and relies only on its guarantees can see unexpected behaviour.

      a: "Throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `limit` is greater than 50."
      b: "Returns `null` when the customer has no orders."
      c: "Throws `InvalidOperationException` if `Warmup()` was not called before."
      d: "Accepts `limit` up to 1000 instead of up to 100."
      e: "Always returns the orders sorted by date."
    optionExplanations:
      d: "This weakens the precondition: the derived class accepts more input than the base class. Calling code passes values from 1 to 100 under the contract, and the derived class handles them the same way, so substitution does not break."

      the base type must stay correct for objects of the subtype. For methods this gives the following rules:

      - **preconditions may only be weakened.** Option a requires `limit <= 50`, although the caller may pass
        80. A call that is valid under the base contract fails. Option d, on the contrary, accepts more, and
        that is safe;

        promised a non-null reference, and the caller gets a `NullReferenceException`. Option e adds a sorting
        guarantee, and that is safe;
      - **no exceptions that the contract does not allow.** Option c throws `InvalidOperationException`,
        which the caller does not expect or handle. In effect it is also a hidden stronger precondition: a
        new obligation to call `Warmup()` first.

      Besides that, a subtype must preserve the invariants of the base type and must not allow state changes
      that the base type forbids (the history rule).

      The C# compiler checks only signatures: all five overrides compile. The contract lives in documentation
      and tests, so it pays to run one shared test suite for the base contract against every derived class.

    answer: |
      1. **Собрать факты.** Для каждого клиента `IRepository` выяснить, какие методы он реально вызывает (поиск

      The project has a shared `IRepository` interface with 25 methods: lookup by key, search, save, delete,
      bulk import, export for reports and more. Six classes implement it, and in three of them some methods
      look like `throw new NotImplementedException();`. Any change to the interface forces edits in all six
      implementations and rebuilds of modules that have nothing to do with the changed methods. Recently the
      reporting module failed in production by calling a method that turned out to be a stub in the injected
      implementation.

      1. **Gather facts.** For each client of `IRepository`, find out which methods it actually calls (find
         usages in the IDE or a small Roslyn analyzer), and for each implementation, which methods work and which
         throw `NotImplementedException`. You get two matrices: "client to methods" and "implementation to
         methods". The groups of methods that clients use together are the future interfaces.
      2. **Design role interfaces.** Along those groups, for example `IOrderReader` (lookup by key and search),
         `IOrderWriter` (save and delete), `IOrderBulkImport` for the bulk load that one module needs. The
         interfaces are expressed in the client's terms and live next to the client, not in a shared
         infrastructure assembly. Do not split down to one method each: what clients always call together
         stays together.
      3. **Migrate incrementally.** First make `IRepository` inherit the new interfaces
         (`interface IRepository : IOrderReader, IOrderWriter, ...`), so everything still compiles. Then move
         clients one at a time to narrow interfaces in their constructors. In DI the same instance is registered
         under several interfaces through a factory, for example
         `services.AddScoped<IOrderReader>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<SqlOrderRepository>())`. Each step is a
         separate small PR with green tests.
      4. **Remove the stubs.** When `IRepository` has no clients left, each implementation declares only the role
         interfaces it really supports, the methods with `NotImplementedException` are deleted, and then
         `IRepository` itself is deleted (it can be marked `[Obsolete]` during the transition).
      5. **Lock it in.** Contract tests for every implementation of every interface; an analyzer rule or a code
         review rule against `NotImplementedException` in production code; an architecture test that keeps new
         modules from depending on the wide interface.
    explanation: |
      Two principles are broken here at once. Interface segregation: clients depend on methods they do not use,
      so a change to any of the 25 methods affects everyone who references `IRepository`, and adding a method
      requires editing all six implementations. Liskov substitution: an implementation that throws instead of
      working does not fulfil the interface contract, and a client cannot know which methods are safe to call.
      The failure shows up only at run time, as it did with the reporting module.

      `NotImplementedException` means unfinished work. Even `NotSupportedException` for an intentionally
      unsupported operation remains a sign of a poor contract unless the contract lets the caller check the
      capability up front, as `ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly` does. Narrow interfaces solve this at the type level:
      an implementation that cannot write simply does not implement `IOrderWriter`, and the compiler will not
      let you pass it where writing is needed.

      Having the wide interface inherit the role interfaces allows a migration without a "big switch": old and
      new clients work side by side. The cost is more types and more DI registrations, so interfaces are cut
      along real groups of calls, not one method per interface. Test fakes also get simpler: a fake for the
      report only has to implement `IOrderReader`.

      In code review the team keeps rejecting the same mistakes: public fields, collection properties with a

      d: "CA1822: Mark members as static"
      e: "CA2007: Consider calling ConfigureAwait on the awaited task"

      Each of the three selected rules closes a way for outside code to bypass a class and change its state
      directly:

      - **CA1051** fires on externally visible (public or protected) instance fields. A field leaves no place
        for validation and does not let you change the data representation later without a breaking API
        change; a property gives you both.
      - **CA2227** fires on a collection property with a public `set`. Through that setter a caller can replace
        the whole collection and bypass the type's logic. The property is made read-only, and the contents are
        changed through methods of the collection or of the owning type.
      - **CA1002** fires on `List<T>` in a public API. `List<T>` is designed for performance, not for
        extension: it has no virtual points through which the owning type could learn about changes. The
        recommended replacements are `Collection<T>`, `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` or
        `KeyedCollection<TKey, TItem>`, where adding and removing items can be intercepted and checked.

      CA1822 and CA2007 are useful, but they solve other problems: the first helps performance, the second
      deals with the synchronization context after `await`. Mixing them into an encapsulation decision makes it
      harder for the team to understand why the restrictions were introduced at all.

      For a lead the rollout matters too: enable the rules through `.editorconfig`
      (`dotnet_diagnostic.CA1051.severity = warning`), start with new code or one project so the team does not
      drown in hundreds of warnings on legacy code, and allow suppressions only with a justification (for
      example a serialization DTO that deliberately needs a public collection setter).
    linkTitles:
      - "CA1051: Do not declare visible instance fields"
      - "CA2227: Collection properties should be read only"
      - "CA1002: Do not expose generic lists"

      Платформенная команда выпускает пакет с классами `BaseController`, `BaseService` и `BaseEntity`, и все
      тридцать сервисов компании обязаны от них наследоваться. В базовых классах живут логирование, обработка

      Почему через несколько лет такая схема превращается в обузу для всей организации и что бы вы предложили
      вместо неё? Как перейти на новую схему, не останавливая тридцать команд?
    hint: Кто на самом деле владеет контрактом базового класса и кто платит, когда платформенная команда меняет его внутренности?

      **Почему это становится обузой**
      - **Базовый класс - это опубликованный фреймворк без дисциплины фреймворка.** Каждый `protected` и

        становятся контрактом, от которого зависят тридцать кодовых баз. Платформенная команда не видит всех
        переопределений и не может понять, какое внутреннее изменение окажется ломающим. Проблема хрупкого
        базового класса перестаёт быть локальной: один рефакторинг `BaseController` ломает сервисы, код которых

      - **Любое изменение превращается в согласованный релиз.** Новая зависимость в конструкторе `BaseService`

      - **Базовые классы разрастаются до god object.** Наследование - единственный канал повторного

  en:
    title: Why do mandatory platform base classes for thirty services become a liability over time?
    prompt: |
      A platform team ships a package with `BaseController`, `BaseService` and `BaseEntity` classes, and all
      thirty services of the company must inherit from them. The base classes contain logging, error handling,
      permission checks, auditing and common entity fields. In the first months this saves time.

      Why does this scheme turn into a liability for the whole organisation after a few years, and what would
      you offer instead? How do you move to the new scheme without stopping thirty teams?
    hint: Who really owns the contract of the base class, and who pays when the platform team changes its internals?
    answer: |
      **Why it becomes a liability**
      - **The base class is a published framework without framework discipline.** Every `protected` and
        `virtual` member, constructor signature and the order in which base methods call overrides becomes a
        contract that thirty codebases depend on. The platform team cannot see all overrides and cannot tell
        which internal change is breaking. The fragile base class problem stops being local: one refactoring of
        `BaseController` breaks services whose code nobody on the platform team has read.
      - **Every change becomes a coordinated release.** A new constructor dependency in `BaseService` forces
        every derived class to change its constructor. Services either upgrade together or pin an old version,
        and several versions of the "platform" with different behaviour run in production.
      - **The base classes grow into god objects.** Inheritance is the only reuse channel, so every team's need
        goes into the shared base. Every service pays for all features at once: dependencies, startup time,
        behaviour it did not ask for.
      - **The single base class slot is taken and the style is frozen.** `BaseController` ties every service to
        MVC controllers and to one way of handling errors. Moving a service to minimal APIs or another pipeline
        means fighting the base class.
      - **`BaseEntity` moves platform decisions into the domain model.** The key type, audit fields and soft
        delete are fixed for every entity of every service. An entity with a `Guid` key, a composite key or no
        auditing does not fit, and changing the base changes the storage schema of thirty databases.
      - **Behaviour is hidden.** Logging, permission checks and transactions in base methods are invisible when
        reading the service code, and a test of a derived class needs the whole environment of the base.

      **What to offer instead**
      - **Cross-cutting HTTP behaviour goes into the pipeline.** `Middleware` and global filters for correlation
        ids, mapping exceptions to problem details and request logging. A service turns them on with one line,
        for example with platform package extension methods such as `builder.AddPlatformDefaults()` and
        `app.UsePlatformDefaults()`, and can disable or replace a single part.
      - **Service behaviour comes through decorators and small interfaces.** Retries, caching and metrics wrap
        interfaces through DI. Instead of `protected` helpers, use narrow abstractions such as `IClock` and
        `ICurrentUser`.
      - **Common entity traits come through small opt-in interfaces.** `IAuditable`, `ISoftDeletable` and a save
        handler in EF Core (a `SaveChangesInterceptor`, global query filters). Each service designs its own
        entities.
      - **Conventions are enforced by project templates, analyzers and architecture tests**, not by a mandatory
        base type.
      - **Where inheritance is truly appropriate, offer a few deliberate extension points:** abstract members with
        a documented contract, everything else `sealed` or non-virtual, semantic versioning and a deprecation
        policy.

      **How to migrate**
      1. Freeze the base classes: no new members.
      2. Build composition equivalents and turn the base classes into thin adapters that delegate to them.
      3. Move services one at a time, starting with those the base hurts most.
      4. Mark the base classes `[Obsolete]` and delete them once the last service has moved.

      Success criterion: a service can upgrade the platform package without changing its own code.
    explanation: |
      The .NET design guidelines call virtual members costly to design, test and maintain: an override can run
      arbitrary code, and the contract of such a member is hard to define precisely. That is why the guidelines
      advise against making members virtual without a good reason and recommend limiting extensibility to what
      is necessary. These rules are written for framework authors, and a platform team with thirty consumer
      services is a framework author, only without the processes that usually protect a framework:
      compatibility review, documented extension points, a versioning policy.

      At the level of one class, a fragile base class is a nuisance for one developer. At the level of an
      organisation, inheritance ties the release schedules, storage decisions and architectural style of thirty
      teams to the decisions of one team. The more derived classes there are, the more expensive any change to
      the base becomes, and the more the platform freezes.

      Composition reverses the direction of control: the service assembles the behaviour it needs from
      independent parts and depends only on their public contracts. A part can be upgraded, replaced or turned
      off without touching the rest. ASP.NET Core `middleware` is a good example: each component solves one
      task, and the application decides the order and content of the pipeline.

      Composition has a cost: explicit registration in each service and some repeated wiring code. One extension
      method and a project template reduce it. Base classes inside one service owned by one team are still fine:
      the problem is mandatory inheritance across teams. A strong answer separates what is truly shared
      (behaviour around the request and infrastructure) from what belongs to the service (the domain model), and
      includes a plan for a gradual transition.

      валидация (команда B) и сохранение в хранилище (команда C, асинхронно и пачками). Цель - не копировать
      данные между этапами. Компоненты принадлежат разным командам, а конвейер будет жить и меняться годами,
      люди в командах будут сменяться.

      Как вы спроектируете владение буферами: кто и когда возвращает буфер в пул, какие типы принимают
      этапы, где допустимо копирование и как обнаруживать нарушения правил?
    hint: |
      Чем `Memory<T>` отличается от того, кто реально отвечает за возврат памяти в пул? И что увидит код, который держит `Memory<T>` на массив, уже выданный пулом другому сообщению?
    answer: |
      1. **Один владелец в каждый момент времени, и это видно по типам.** Арендованный буфер оборачивается
         во владельца: `IMemoryOwner<byte>` (например, из `MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent`) или тип сообщения,
         который его содержит. В любой момент буфером владеет ровно один компонент. Владелец либо освобождает
         буфер (`Dispose`), либо передаёт владение дальше, но не то и другое сразу, и освобождение происходит
         ровно один раз. Параметр типа `IMemoryOwner<T>` (или типа сообщения-владельца) в сигнатуре означает
         «метод забирает владение»: после вызова вызывающий код буфер больше не трогает.
      2. **Потребители получают аренду (lease), а не владение.**
         - синхронные этапы (декодирование, валидация) принимают `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`: это `ref struct`,
           и компилятор сам не даёт сохранить её в куче или пронести через `await`, поэтому аренда гарантированно
           заканчивается на выходе из метода;
         - асинхронные этапы принимают `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` и пользуются им только до завершения
           возвращённой `Task`;
         - метод, который принимает `Memory<T>` и возвращает `void`, не использует его после возврата;
           тип, получающий `Memory<T>` в конструкторе, делает потребителями все свои методы и растягивает аренду
           на время жизни объекта - на границах между командами такие контракты лучше не допускать;
         - этапы, которые только читают, получают read-only типы.
      3. **Копировать там, где контракт нельзя обеспечить.** Всё, что переживает вызов: очереди, кэши,
         фоновые задачи, логирование содержимого, накопление пачек при сохранении, повторные попытки. Здесь
         либо явно передаётся владение (этап сохранения принимает владельца и освобождает его после завершения
         записи), либо данные копируются в память, которой компонент владеет сам (`ToArray` или собственный
         арендованный буфер). Правило: без копирования внутри компонента, явная передача владения или копия на его
         границе. Решение подтверждается замером: одна копия в несколько килобайт рядом с записью в базу
         обычно незаметна.
      4. **Раздача нескольким потребителям.** Если один буфер нужен нескольким параллельным потребителям,
         модель одного владельца не подходит: либо копия на каждого потребителя, либо владелец со счётчиком ссылок
         (`Interlocked`, последний освободивший возвращает буфер). Счётчик ссылок - крайняя мера: лишнее или
         пропущенное освобождение даёт те же ошибки, только реже.
      5. **Сделать нарушения видимыми.**
         - в тестовом и отладочном режиме - пул, который выдаёт новые массивы и заполняет возвращённые буферы
           «ядовитым» шаблоном, и обёртка-владелец, которая бросает `ObjectDisposedException` при обращении
           после освобождения и обнаруживает повторное освобождение;
         - нагрузочные и параллельные тесты, контрактные тесты на каждой границе между командами;
         - контракт владения записан в ADR и в чек-листе code review, а не держится в памяти авторов.
      6. **Утечка лучше порчи данных.** Невозвращённый в `ArrayPool<T>` массив просто соберёт сборщик мусора,
         это стоит только производительности. Возврат слишком рано или дважды портит чужие данные. Поэтому при
         неясном владении буфер не возвращают, а не возвращают «на всякий случай».
    explanation: |
      `Memory<T>` - это только ссылка на массив (или `MemoryManager<T>`), смещение и длина. Он не владеет памятью
      и не знает, что буфер вернули в пул. После возврата пул выдаёт тот же массив следующему арендатору, а
      старый `Memory<T>` остаётся для среды выполнения совершенно корректным: исключения нет. Чтение видит
      данные чужого сообщения, запись портит чужое сообщение. Ошибка проявляется под нагрузкой, плохо
      воспроизводится и может навсегда попасть в хранилище. Повторный возврат ещё хуже: один массив может
      оказаться у двух арендаторов одновременно.

      Рекомендации Microsoft по `Memory<T>` и `Span<T>` вводят именно эти понятия: у буфера один владелец,
      который управляет временем жизни, потребители и аренда - время, в течение которого потребитель может
      пользоваться буфером. Владельца `IMemoryOwner<T>` нужно либо освободить, либо передать, но не то и другое,
      а параметр `IMemoryOwner<T>` в API означает принятие владения. Архитектурная задача в том, чтобы эти правила
      пережили смену команд. Поэтому владение выражается в сигнатурах, а не в комментариях: ограничения
      `ref struct` для `Span<T>` - единственная аренда, которую проверяет компилятор, а тип `IMemoryOwner<T>` в
      параметре явно показывает передачу владения. Там, где ни типы, ни компилятор аренду не ограничивают,
      безопаснее заплатить за копию, чем рисковать тихой порчей данных.

      Ещё две детали: пул может выдать буфер больше запрошенного размера, поэтому дальше передаётся срез нужной
      длины, а не весь буфер; и `ArrayPool<T>` по умолчанию не очищает возвращённые массивы, поэтому для
      чувствительных данных используют `Return(array, clearArray: true)`.

      - "Рекомендации по использованию Memory<T> и Span<T>"
      - "Интерфейс IMemoryOwner<T>"
      - "Класс ArrayPool<T>"

    title: How do you design ownership of pooled buffers in a zero-copy message pipeline that different teams evolve over years?
    prompt: |
      The network layer rents buffers from a pool and passes each message through a pipeline: decoding (team A),
      validation (team B) and persistence to storage (team C, asynchronous and batched). The goal is not to copy
      data between the stages. The components belong to different teams, and the pipeline will live and change
      for years while people on the teams come and go.

      How do you design buffer ownership: who returns a buffer to the pool and when, which types do the stages
      accept, where is copying acceptable, and how do you detect rule violations?
    hint: |
      How does a `Memory<T>` differ from whoever is actually responsible for returning the memory to the pool? And what does code see if it holds a `Memory<T>` over an array that the pool has already handed to another message?
    answer: |
      1. **One owner at a time, visible in the types.** The rented buffer is wrapped in an owner:
         `IMemoryOwner<byte>` (for example from `MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent`) or a message type that holds it.
         At any moment exactly one component owns the buffer. The owner either releases it (`Dispose`) or
         transfers ownership, never both, and release happens exactly once. A parameter of type `IMemoryOwner<T>`
         (or of the owning message type) in a signature means "this method takes ownership": after the call the
         caller does not touch the buffer.
      2. **Consumers get leases, not ownership.**
         - synchronous stages (decoding, validation) take `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`: it is a `ref struct`, and the
           compiler itself prevents storing it on the heap or carrying it across `await`, so the lease is
           guaranteed to end when the method returns;
         - asynchronous stages take `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` and use it only until the returned `Task` completes;
         - a method that accepts `Memory<T>` and returns `void` does not use it after it returns; a type that
           receives `Memory<T>` in its constructor makes all its methods consumers and stretches the lease to the
           lifetime of the object - avoid such contracts at boundaries between teams;
         - stages that only read get read-only types.
      3. **Copy where the contract cannot be enforced.** Anything that outlives the call: queues, caches,
         background tasks, payload logging, batching in persistence, retries. There, either ownership is
         transferred explicitly (the persistence stage takes the owner and releases it after the write completes),
         or the data is copied into memory the component owns itself (`ToArray` or its own rented buffer). The rule:
         zero-copy inside a component, explicit transfer or a copy at its edge. Confirm the decision by measuring:
         one copy of a few kilobytes next to a database write is usually noise.
      4. **Fan-out to several consumers.** If one buffer is needed by several parallel consumers, the single-owner
         model does not fit: either a copy per consumer, or a reference-counted owner (`Interlocked`, the last
         release returns the buffer). Reference counting is a last resort: an extra or missed release produces the
         same bugs, just less often.
      5. **Make violations visible.**
         - in test and debug mode, a pool that hands out fresh arrays and fills returned buffers with a poison
           pattern, and an owner wrapper that throws `ObjectDisposedException` on access after release and detects
           a double release;
         - load and concurrency tests, and contract tests at every boundary between teams;
         - the ownership contract is recorded in an ADR and in the code review checklist, not kept in the memory
           of its authors.
      6. **A leak is better than corruption.** An array that is never returned to `ArrayPool<T>` is simply
         collected by the garbage collector, which costs only performance. Returning too early or twice corrupts
         someone else's data. So when ownership is unclear, the buffer is not returned, rather than returned
         "just in case".
    explanation: |
      A `Memory<T>` is only a reference to an array (or a `MemoryManager<T>`), an offset and a length. It does not
      own the memory and does not know that the buffer was returned to the pool. After the return, the pool hands
      the same array to the next renter, while the old `Memory<T>` is still perfectly valid as far as the runtime
      is concerned: there is no exception. Reads see another message's data, writes corrupt another message. The
      bug shows up under load, is hard to reproduce and can end up in storage permanently. A double return is even
      worse: one array can end up with two renters at the same time.

      The Microsoft guidelines for `Memory<T>` and `Span<T>` introduce exactly these concepts: a buffer has one
      owner who manages its lifetime, consumers, and a lease - the period during which a consumer may use the
      buffer. An `IMemoryOwner<T>` must be either disposed or transferred, but not both, and an `IMemoryOwner<T>`
      parameter in an API means accepting ownership. The architectural task is to make these rules survive team
      changes. That is why ownership is expressed in signatures, not in comments: the `ref struct` restrictions of
      `Span<T>` are the only lease the compiler checks, and an `IMemoryOwner<T>` parameter type makes the transfer
      of ownership explicit. Where neither the types nor the compiler limit the lease, paying for a copy is safer
      than risking silent data corruption.

      Two more details: a pool may return a buffer larger than requested, so the stages receive a slice of the
      needed length rather than the whole buffer; and `ArrayPool<T>` does not clear returned arrays by default, so
      for sensitive data use `Return(array, clearArray: true)`.
    linkTitles:
      - "Memory<T> and Span<T> usage guidelines"
      - "IMemoryOwner<T> interface"
      - "ArrayPool<T> class"
